_work.title: Kunh al-Murād fī Wafq al-Aʻdād — Treatise on Magic Squares (Princeton, Third Series no. 455)
_work.blurb: A Persian-language treatise on the construction and use of magic squares (wafq al-aʻdād), attributed to Yaʻqūb ibn Muḥammad al-Ṭāʻūsī and also to Sharaf al-Dīn ʻAlī al-Yazdī (d. 858/1454), organized in three sections (lawḥ). Held at Princeton University Library (Third Series no. 455), 89 leaves (178 pages), 18th–19th century CE, purchased from Smitskamp Oriental Antiquarian in 2001 and bound in red leather over paper boards with blind-stamped decoration. The manuscript is a systematic encyclopaedia of wafq construction, containing an extraordinary range of magic square formats: dense full-page letter-wafq grids where each cell is subdivided into sub-compartments and filled with Arabic letter combinations; large-cell numeric wafq in a sparse arithmetic-exposition format showing the raw integer values; combinatorial lookup tables for computing wafq parameters; labeled construction tables that reveal the derivation method step by step; multi-table pages presenting six or more wafq configurations simultaneously; and tricolor letter-wafq grids using red, black, and olive-green ink to color-code cells by magical correspondence category. Some tables are notched or L-shaped where the grid outgrew the page. The three-color wafq is characteristic of the Persianate tradition of color-coded wafq encyclopaedias; each full-page grid functions simultaneously as a mathematical object and a talismanic reference tool.
_work.rights: Public Domain — 18th–19th century CE manuscript. Princeton University Library.
_work.creator: Ṭāʻūsī, Yaʻqūb ibn Muḥammad (also attr. Sharaf al-Dīn ʻAlī al-Yazdī, d. 1454)

entries.title: Three Wafq Magic Squares Embedded in Prose Text (Kunh al-Murād, f. 6a)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, red ink
entries.summary: A page of Persian prose text from the Kunh al-Murād fī Wafq al-Aʻdād (Princeton Third Series no. 455) with three distinct wafq magic square diagrams embedded within the running text — a large letter-wafq in the upper right, and two smaller wafq grids (one numeric, one letter-combination) in the lower portion, all integrated into the prose columns around them. This explanatory-text format is the didactic mode of the wafq treatise: the scribe does not dedicate an entire page to a diagram but instead inserts each wafq inline as the text introduces or defines it, surrounding the grid with the Persian prose explanation of its construction method, correspondence, or operative use. The chapter heading in red ink at the top of the page (dar tartīb-i wafq, 'on the arrangement of the wafq,' or similar) introduces the section. The three grids on this folio likely represent a progression: first a worked example of a basic type, then its two derived variants, with the text explaining the transformation between them. This embedded-diagram format is the standard pedagogical format of Persian mathematical and magical manuscript treatises, where diagrams are learning tools embedded in prose rather than stand-alone reference objects.

entries.title: Massive Full-Page Letter-Wafq Grid — Largest in Manuscript (Kunh al-Murād, f. 17a)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, red ink
entries.summary: The largest and most dense wafq diagram in the Kunh al-Murād fī Wafq al-Aʻdād (Princeton Third Series no. 455) — a massive letter-wafq filling nearly the entire page, with a bordered rectangular grid approximately 18 columns × 20 rows, each cell subdivided horizontally into two sub-cells containing Arabic letter combinations written in alternating black and red ink. The outer border of the grid is a double-ruled frame. Column header labels in red ink run across the top of the grid, identifying the category or parameter associated with each column. The page number '17' appears in the upper margin. With roughly 360 sub-cells each containing distinct letter combinations, this grid represents one of the most computationally ambitious wafq tables in the Persian tradition: a complete system mapping letter combinations onto a 18×20 wafq structure — far larger than the 5×5 or 7×7 wafq found in most Islamic magic treatises. This scale is characteristic of the Kunh al-Murād's encyclopaedic ambition, providing a practitioner with the full combinatorial system rather than just a representative example.

entries.title: Large-Cell Numeric Wafq Tables — Arithmetic Exposition Format (Kunh al-Murād, f. 22a)
entries.summary: A page from the Kunh al-Murād fī Wafq al-Aʻdād (Princeton Third Series no. 455) containing two numeric wafq tables in a radically different visual format from the dense letter-grids that dominate the manuscript: a large-cell arithmetic-exposition style where each cell is spacious and contains a single readable Persian/Arabic numeral, making the integer values of the magic square clearly legible. The upper table is approximately 5×4 cells with large numerals; the lower table is larger (~9×8 cells) with somewhat smaller but still clearly readable numerals. Both tables are bordered with ruled frames. This sparse, large-cell format is the mathematical counterpart to the dense letter-wafq: instead of encoding operative letter combinations, these pages expose the arithmetic skeleton — the actual number values whose row/column/diagonal sums are all equal (the defining property of a magic square). In Islamic wafq science, the numeric wafq is the foundation from which letter-wafq and word-wafq are derived by substituting abjad-value correspondences for each number. This page is therefore a foundational reference: the practitioner starts here with the numbers, then uses the abjad conversion table to produce the letter configurations shown on other pages.

entries.title: Combinatorial Wafq Lookup Table with Labeled Row and Column Headers (Kunh al-Murād, f. 31a)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, red ink
entries.summary: A structurally unique page from the Kunh al-Murād fī Wafq al-Aʻdād (Princeton Third Series no. 455) containing multiple interlocking numeric tables in a combinatorial arrangement that differs fundamentally from the standard magic-square format of other pages. The main table (occupying the upper and left portion of the page) has a labeled header row in red ink across the top — listing parameter names or category identifiers — and labeled row identifiers on the right side, with Persian numerals filling the cells of the body. Below and to the right, a second smaller table continues the combinatorial scheme. The page number '31' appears in the upper margin. This combinatorial lookup table structure is used in wafq science for systematic correspondence: given a particular input (planet, letter, magical purpose, or number), the practitioner reads across the labeled rows and columns to find the appropriate wafq configuration parameter. The presence of multiple distinct tables on a single page, each with its own header system, suggests this folio belongs to a section on the computational derivation of wafq — the mathematical method for constructing a magic square from given correspondences rather than simply copying a pre-computed table. Column totals or check sums may appear at the bottom of the main table.

entries.title: Notched Large Letter-Wafq Grid with Text Inset (Kunh al-Murād, f. 38a)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, red ink
entries.summary: A large letter-wafq from the Kunh al-Murād fī Wafq al-Aʻdād (Princeton Third Series no. 455) with an unusual notched or L-shaped outline — the wafq grid does not fill a perfect rectangle but instead has a rectangular section cut from one corner, where a short block of Persian prose text is inset within the grid frame. This notched format occurs when the scribe began laying out the wafq grid and needed to accommodate an explanatory text block within the same page frame; instead of placing the text above or below the grid, it is inset as a notch within the grid's corner. Row identifiers or labels appear on the right-hand margin. The wafq cells themselves contain Arabic letter combinations in black and red ink in the subdivided cell format common to letter-wafq throughout this manuscript. Page 38 is in the middle of the manuscript's main wafq encyclopaedia section, suggesting this notched wafq represents one of the more complex or unusual configurations that required additional explanation. The irregular shape — a grid with a rectangular hole — is visually distinctive and underscores the manuscript's functional character: the design accommodates mathematical content rather than striving for visual regularity.

entries.title: Full-Page Letter-Wafq Grid — Standard Format (Kunh al-Murād, f. 45a)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, red ink
entries.summary: A canonical full-page letter-wafq from the Kunh al-Murād fī Wafq al-Aʻdād (Princeton Third Series no. 455), representing the standard format that recurs throughout the manuscript: a double-bordered rectangular grid occupying most of the page (with a short caption line in Persian at the bottom and the folio number '45' at the top), divided into rows and columns of sub-cells each containing Arabic letter combinations in alternating black and red ink. The wafq has no notches, irregular shapes, or inset text — it is a clean, complete grid. The caption at the bottom (in red ink) names this wafq type, its operative purpose, or the section (lawḥ) of the treatise it belongs to. This standard full-page format is the workhorse of the Kunh al-Murād: each wafq of this type is a complete reference tool, a page the practitioner turns to and reads directly, locating the appropriate cell by row and column coordinates to find the letter combination needed for a specific talisman or charm. The regularity of this format across many pages of the manuscript reflects the encyclopaedic project: systematic coverage of all wafq types in a uniform reference format.

entries.title: Letter-Wafq Grid with Persian Prose Header (Kunh al-Murād, f. 59a)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, red ink
entries.summary: A page from the Kunh al-Murād fī Wafq al-Aʻdād (Princeton Third Series no. 455) with a substantial Persian prose header block occupying approximately the top quarter of the page (about 4–5 lines of text in nastaliq script, with red ink for emphasis and chapter headings), followed by a large letter-wafq grid filling the remaining three-quarters. The text header introduces or names the specific wafq that follows, identifying its lawḥ (section), its operative purpose, the planet or letter-class it corresponds to, and the conditions for its use. This text-then-grid layout is the primary didactic format of the wafq treatise: theory precedes practice, and each new wafq type is introduced by its name and description before being displayed. The grid itself is a standard letter-wafq with subdivided cells and alternating red/black letter combinations. This format, where a block of Persian prose frames and authorizes the diagram, is characteristic of the Kunh al-Murād's pedagogical approach: the manuscript does not merely catalogue wafq tables but teaches their use and identification.

entries.title: Labeled Numeric Construction Table with Row Sums — Wafq Derivation (Kunh al-Murād, f. 67a)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, red ink
entries.summary: The most mathematically explicit page in the Kunh al-Murād fī Wafq al-Aʻdād (Princeton Third Series no. 455), containing a labeled numeric construction table that reveals the step-by-step derivation method for a magic square rather than simply displaying the finished product. The main table (left half of the page) has labeled rows in Persian — identifying each row by ordinal number (first, second, third...) or parameter name — with a totals row at the bottom showing column sums and a grand total. A second section on the right contains a Persian prose block alongside a smaller wafq grid. The labeled construction table is the methodological core of the wafq treatise: it shows HOW a magic square is built, not just what it looks like. In the Islamic wafq tradition, constructing a magic square from a given magical target (a planet, a letter, a divine name, a numerical value) requires a specific computational procedure — you begin with seed values, apply transformations, fill each row according to a rule, and verify the sums. This page captures that computational procedure in tabular form. The presence of row sums and column totals visible at the bottom border is mathematically diagnostic: these are the 'magic constant' verification sums confirming that the wafq is correctly computed.

entries.title: Tricolor Letter-Wafq — Red, Black, and Olive-Green Ink Coding (Kunh al-Murād, f. 75a)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, red, black, and olive-green ink
entries.summary: A full-page letter-wafq from the Kunh al-Murād fī Wafq al-Aʻdād (Princeton Third Series no. 455) with tricolor ink coding — each sub-cell's letter combination is written in one of three distinct inks: black, red, or olive-green/yellow-green. The color assignment is systematic and non-random: each color encodes a categorical attribute of the letter combination in that cell — its planet (the three inks may correspond to three planetary groupings), its element (fire/air/water), its operative property (talismanic, protective, destructive), or its correspondence class within the letter-science (huruf) system. The tricolor wafq is the most visually distinctive format in this manuscript and is specific to the Persianate tradition of color-coded wafq encyclopaedias; it is rarely found in Arabic-script wafq manuscripts from the Arab heartland but is well-documented in Persian and Ottoman contexts. The three-color system allows a practitioner to use the wafq as a lookup tool for BOTH the letter combination AND its categorical assignment simultaneously — scanning the grid by color first, then by position, to find the specific cell needed for a given operative purpose. The colors are created using three separate inks: carbon black, iron gall red, and a copper-based green or gall-iron olive pigment.

entries.title: Full-Page Tricolor Letter-Wafq with Column Category Headers (Kunh al-Murād, f. 77a)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, red, black, and olive-green ink
entries.summary: A full-page tricolor letter-wafq from the Kunh al-Murād fī Wafq al-Aʻdād (Princeton Third Series no. 455), distinguished from the adjacent tricolor wafq on f. 75a by the presence of labeled column category headers across the top of the grid — each column is headed by a label in red ink identifying the category, planet, letter group, or parameter that governs the letter combinations in that column. The three ink colors (black, red, olive-green) fill the wafq cells below the headers. The column headers are the KEY for reading the tricolor system: they name the categorical system that the color coding embodies. By reading the header of a column and matching its color to the color of the cells, a practitioner could decode the color-coding rule and use it on any other tricolor wafq page in the manuscript. This page is therefore meta-informational: it is both a wafq reference table AND a legend explaining the color system. The headers across the top are written in a larger, clearer hand than the cell contents, and some are highlighted with a red or gold ink frame. A short Persian caption line appears at the top of the page above the headers (folio number '77' in the margin).

entries.title: Six Wafq Tables on One Page — Multi-Configuration Panel (Kunh al-Murād, f. 79a)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, red ink
entries.summary: The most information-dense page in the Kunh al-Murād fī Wafq al-Aʻdād (Princeton Third Series no. 455) — a single folio containing SIX distinct wafq magic square grids arranged in a structured multi-panel layout. The page is divided into two horizontal halves: the upper half contains four smaller wafq tables arranged in a 2×2 grid (two rows, two columns), and the lower half contains two larger letter-wafq tables in the dense subdivided-cell format. The upper four tables use a numeric or sparser letter format; the lower two use the dense tricolor letter-wafq format with subdivided sub-cells. Folio number '79' appears in the upper margin, and a short Persian caption or header line runs above the arrangement. This multi-configuration panel presents the variant configurations of a single wafq base — in the Islamic wafq tradition, a base magic square generates multiple variant squares by rotation (4 rotations × 2 reflections = 8 basic variants), digit-rearrangement, or column-row transposition. The six grids on this page likely represent a selected subset of variants for a particular wafq type, allowing the practitioner to choose the most appropriate configuration for a given operative purpose without having to compute the variants themselves. This is the reference-book function of the wafq encyclopaedia at its most compressed.
